mcqs.question: An internal call happens 50,000 times/sec between two backend services with one fixed request/response shape. Which style best fits, and why?
options: GraphQL, because it is the most flexible and modern option available
gRPC, because compact binary payloads over HTTP/2 minimize serialization cost at this call volume
REST with JSON, because it is the easiest to inspect with curl during debugging
REST with XML, because it enforces the strictest schema of the three
mcqs.explanation: There's one caller and one fixed shape, so GraphQL's flexibility is wasted overhead, not a benefit. At 50,000 calls/sec, gRPC's compact protobuf payloads and HTTP/2 multiplexing meaningfully cut serialization and network cost. REST's readability is a real plus at low volume, not at this scale, and XML isn't more strict than a protobuf schema.

mcqs.question: Why does switching order-service-to-inventory-service calls from REST/JSON to gRPC/protobuf matter at 20,000 calls/sec but barely matter at 20 calls/sec?
options: Protobuf only produces valid output above a certain call-volume threshold
gRPC requires a minimum request rate to establish its HTTP/2 connection
JSON parsing is disabled by most runtimes above 1,000 requests/sec
The per-call savings in payload size and serialization cost are fixed, so they compound into significant total cost only when multiplied by high volume
mcqs.explanation: The per-call savings from protobuf and HTTP/2 are roughly constant regardless of traffic; what changes is the total impact, since a fixed saving times 20,000 calls/sec is significant CPU and network cost, while the same saving times 20 calls/sec is noise. Protobuf and gRPC work identically at any volume — there's no threshold or disabled behavior involved.

mcqs.question: What does GraphQL trade away in exchange for letting each client request its own shape of data?
options: The simple per-resource HTTP caching and rate-limiting that URL-based routing gives REST almost for free
The ability to serve more than one client type from the same backend
Support for mutations — GraphQL can only read data, never write it
Compatibility with mobile clients, which cannot send GraphQL queries
mcqs.explanation: Because GraphQL typically exposes one endpoint that accepts arbitrary queries, you lose the easy per-URL caching and rate-limiting REST gets from routing. GraphQL is specifically built to serve multiple client shapes, it fully supports mutations, and mobile clients can and do send GraphQL queries.

mcqs.question: A GraphQL query nesting 8 resources deep just timed out from an N+1-style explosion of backend calls. What are the two concrete fixes?
options: Switch the entire API to REST, and cache every possible query result
Disable nested queries entirely, and require clients to make one flat request per resource
Increase the gateway's timeout, and add more backend server replicas
A query complexity/depth limit at the gateway, and dataloader-style batching so nested resolvers don't each fire their own backend call
mcqs.explanation: A complexity/depth limit stops runaway queries before they reach resolvers, and dataloader batching collapses per-resolver calls into a handful of batched fetches, fixing the N+1 pattern directly. Switching to REST or disabling nesting throws away GraphQL's value proposition entirely, and raising timeouts or adding replicas just delays the same explosion rather than fixing it.
